web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Syllabus Overview
web_content_rtb__content.value:
Organisation of Geography Elective 7–10

Figure 1 shows the organisation of Geography Elective 7–10.

Image long description: Geographical concepts, Geographical inquiry skills and Geographical tools appear from left to the right at the top of the diagram. The Geographical concepts include place, space, environment, interconnection, scale, sustainability and change. The Geographical inquiry skills include acquiring, processing and communicating geographical information. The Geographical tools include maps, fieldwork, data and statistics, spatial technologies, and additional geographical representations. These 3 groups are connected by a line to Thinking and working geographically and to Knowledge, understanding and skills, to demonstrate the interconnected nature of the learning. Encompassed within this line are 9 focus areas. Under the heading of Focus on physical geography are the focus areas Planet Earth, Extreme environments, Oceanography and Interactions and patterns across a continent. Under the heading Focus on human geography are the focus areas Global citizenship, Geopolitics, Australia’s neighbours and Primary production. The ninth focus area School-developed option overlaps both Focus on physical geography and Focus on human geography.

Life Skills outcomes and content

Protocols for collaborating with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Communities

NESA is committed to working in partnership with Aboriginal Communities and supporting teachers, schools and schooling sectors to improve educational outcomes for young people.

It is important to respect appropriate ways of interacting with Aboriginal Communities and Cultural material when teachers plan, program and implement learning experiences that focus on Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Priorities.

Indigenous Cultural and Intellectual Property (ICIP) protocols need to be followed. Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ ICIP protocols include Cultural Knowledges, Cultural Expression and Cultural Property and documentation of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ identities and lived experiences. It is important to recognise the diversity and complexity of different Cultural groups in NSW, as protocols may differ between local Aboriginal Communities.

Teachers should work in partnership with Elders, parents, Community members, Cultural Knowledge Holders, or a local, regional or state Aboriginal Education Consultative Group. It is important to respect Elders and the roles of men and women. Local Aboriginal Peoples should be invited to share their Cultural Knowledges with students and staff when engaging with Aboriginal histories and Cultural Practices.

Creating written texts supports learning

The development of the Geography Elective 7–10 Syllabus follows Recommendation 2: ‘Clarify and strengthen writing content in syllabus documents’ from Teaching writing: report of the thematic review of writing (NESA 2018).

Creating written texts facilitates learning as it promotes explicitness, encourages the integration of ideas, supports reflection, fosters personal engagement and aids learners to think about the significance and implication of ideas. Each subject has particular and specific writing demands relevant for communicating within and about the discipline. Writing about content enhances understanding across subjects and stages.

The secondary curriculum includes:

  • systematic development of expectations for creating written texts which align with the English K–10 Syllabus (2022)
  • explicit writing content to support students to become fluent creators of texts and to deepen their understanding of the subject area
  • opportunities to practise the process of creating written texts to develop and communicate knowledge, understanding and ideas
  • a focus on development of word consciousness and precise use of subject-specific terminology.

Creating written texts refers to the act of composing and constructing a text for a particular purpose, audience and context.

Various methods of transcription may be employed, and a student’s preferred communication form(s) should be considered when teaching.

Balance of content

The outcomes describe the knowledge, understanding and skills that students are expected to demonstrate as a result of teaching and learning. Teachers should use the outcomes to determine the scope of learning for the content included in each focus area.

The amount of content associated with a given outcome is not necessarily indicative of the amount of time spent engaging with the respective outcome. Teachers use formative and summative assessment to determine instructional priorities and the time needed for students to demonstrate expected outcomes.

In considering the intended learning, teachers make decisions about the sequence and emphasis to be given to particular groups of content based on the needs and abilities of their students.

course_content.name: 📜 Course Description
course_content.value:
Courses

The Geography Elective 7–10 Syllabus includes 4 elective courses:

  • Geography Elective 200-hour elective
  • Geography Elective 100-hour elective
  • Geography Elective Life Skills 200-hour elective
  • Geography Elective Life Skills 100-hour elective.

Focus of learning

In Geography Elective, students investigate physical and human environments, geographical processes and contemporary geographical challenges. They develop knowledge about the interactions between people, places and environments across a range of scales, and respond to real-world challenges in an informed manner. Students apply geographical concepts to guide investigations and propose explanations for patterns, relationships and variations in geographical phenomena. They engage with a range of geographical tools including maps, fieldwork, data and graphs, spatial technologies and other geographical representations, to acquire, process and communicate information.

What students learn

Students learn about the natural systems that influence Earth’s landscapes, climates and ecosystems by investigating physical geography in the focus areas Planet Earth, Extreme environments, Oceanography and Interactions and patterns across a continent. Additionally, students learn about the social, cultural, political and economic systems that shape the ways people interact with, organise and manage places and environments in the focus areas Global citizenship, Geopolitics, Australia’s neighbours and Primary production.

Students extend their knowledge about environmental and social sustainability, and the vital roles played by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and other Indigenous communities in their custodianship of Country and Place. They develop an understanding of contemporary geographical issues and build their capacity to be active, informed and responsible global citizens.

Course requirements

Safety and risk management

Schools are required to ensure they follow safety and risk management in delivering the Geography Elective 7–10 Syllabus.

100-hour and 200-hour elective course requirements

Geography Elective 7–10 may be studied as a 100-hour or a 200-hour course. The content available for Stage 4 is identical to that available for Stage 5. When teaching the course in Stage 4, the Stage 5 outcomes may be adjusted as appropriate to the needs of students in Years 7 and 8. Advice is provided to support teachers.

All outcomes must be programmed for 100-hour and 200-hour courses.

100-hour elective course requirements

Students are required to undertake:

  • at least ONE focus area with a focus on physical geography
  • at least ONE focus area with a focus on human geography
  • at least ONE additional focus area to meet the 100-hour requirement.
200-hour elective course requirements

Students are required to undertake:

  • at least ONE focus area with a focus on physical geography
  • at least ONE focus area with a focus on human geography
  • at least THREE additional focus areas to meet the 200-hour requirement.

Across a 100-hour course or a 200-hour Stage 5 course, students may study only ONE school-developed option.

Geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools

The geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools are to be integrated with the content of the Geography Elective 7–10 Syllabus.

Fieldwork: Fieldwork is an essential component of the Geography Elective 7–10 course. All students undertaking Geography Elective 7–10 must complete approximately 10 hours of fieldwork per stage, in addition to the fieldwork requirements outlined in the Geography 7–10 course. Fieldwork could include pre-fieldwork activities and post-fieldwork activities.

Students with disability may require adjustments in order to engage with inquiry skills and tools, including fieldwork.

Life Skills – 100-hour and 200-hour elective courses

For Geography Elective Life Skills:

  • Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Geography Elective 7–10 Life Skills outcomes.
  • Outcomes and content should be selected to meet the particular needs of individual students.
  • The focus areas provide possible frameworks for addressing the Geography Elective 7–10 Life Skills outcomes and content and are suggestions only. Teachers have the flexibility to select, group and sequence outcomes and content to meet the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students.
  • Fieldwork is essential to the study of Geography Elective 7–10 Life Skills. All students should have the opportunity to participate in fieldwork to develop their understanding and demonstrate achievement of Geography Elective 7–10 Life Skills outcomes.
  • Students with disability may require adjustments in order to engage with inquiry skills and tools, including fieldwork.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Students with disability can access the syllabus outcomes and content in a range of ways. Decisions regarding curriculum options should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

Some students with intellectual disability may find the Years 7–10 Life Skills outcomes and content the most appropriate option to follow in Stage 4 and/or Stage 5. Before determining whether a student is eligible to undertake a course based on Life Skills outcomes and content, consideration should be given to other ways of assisting the student to engage with the Stage 4 and/or Stage 5 outcomes, or prior stage outcomes if appropriate. This assistance may include a range of adjustments to teaching, learning and assessment activities.

Life Skills outcomes cannot be taught in combination with other outcomes from the same subject. Teachers select specific Life Skills outcomes to teach based on the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of each student. Students are required to demonstrate achievement of one or more Life Skills outcomes.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

By exploring examples of primary production, such as agriculture, mining, fishing, forestry and farming, students develop an understanding of the role of primary production in communities and for daily living. Through exploring the use of natural resources in primary production, students deepen their understanding of sustainability.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching ways to conserve natural resources, students are required to demonstrate ways to manage and protect a place or environment. Students sort cards under one of 2 headings, Conserve or Waste, applying scenarios in primary production, such as using solar panels or overwatering.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Environment – diverse environments have a range of natural resources used in primary production.
  • Sustainability – the ability of environments to support life for the future is dependent on the strategies used to manage natural resources sustainably.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, topographic maps, thematic mapsSector graphs, climate graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, geographic information systems (GIS)Tactile graphics and models, diagrams, infographics, flow charts, sketches (such as field sketches, line drawings and photo sketches)

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Examples of fieldwork could include visiting a local farm, farmers’ market, regional show (e.g. Royal Easter Show), school garden or agriculture plot, or supermarket chain to trace the journey of the food or crop being grown.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

  • What is primary production and what are the main types of primary production in NSW?
  • Why are some areas of NSW more suitable to primary production than others?
  • How is water managed in farming, particularly in drought-stricken areas?

Investigative study

Through the investigative study, students have the opportunity to explore ONE activity in relation to primary production operating on a local, regional or global scale. For example:

  • Local – local producers for farmers’ markets, a small apiary selling to local consumers
  • Regional – dairy farmers on the South Coast of NSW
  • Global – beef or wool from the Central West and Monaro regions for export.

Connecting with Stage 5 Geography Elective

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography Elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Sustainable practices associated with agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry
The teacher introduces sustainable practices in the agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry industries and identifies the key practices the primary producer can use to minimise environmental impacts, such as crop rotation, reforestation or solar power.

Students select either a local, regional or global example of primary producers. Students use a comparison matrix to analyse the sustainability of each primary producer’s practice.

Life Skills

  • Management of primary production activities to protect the environment
The teacher introduces sustainable practices of interest to students in the agriculture, mining, fishing or forestry industry. The teacher identifies the key practices the primary producer can use to minimise environmental impacts, such as crop rotation, reforestation or solar power.

Students use a graphic organiser to sort images and identify the ways human activity in primary production activities can harm or protect the environment. Alternatively, students create a poster that communicates how primary production industries can protect the environment.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the role of primary production in providing essential resources, sustaining economies and supporting livelihoods. They learn about the spatial distribution and processes involved in agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry, and learn about global patterns of production. Students investigate the economic significance of primary production, including technological innovations, the influence of multinational organisations and the contribution of primary industries to local and global communities. They consider environmental impacts, challenges related to resource use and sustainable practices that aim to reduce harm and secure future production.

Key terms

  • agriculture
  • fishing
  • forestry
  • mining
  • primary production

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Space: The distribution of agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry activities and how physical and human factors influence where and how they occur.
  • Sustainability: The environmental, social and economic implications of primary production practices and the need to adopt sustainable approaches to ensure long-term resource security.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How does primary production support communities and economies at local, national and global scales?
  • What factors influence the spatial patterns and processes of agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry around the world?
  • What are the environmental, social and economic impacts of primary production and how are they being addressed?
  • How is innovation shaping the future of primary production and what strategies can ensure sustainability in primary production?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Primary production content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, sketch maps, précis maps, topographic maps, land use maps, cartogram maps, graduated or proportional symbol mapsSector graphs, climate graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, geographic information systems (GIS)Tactile graphics and models, diagrams, flow charts, infographics, sketches

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials that explore different types of primary production such as agriculture, forestry, fishing and mining across diverse environments, and highlight environmental impacts, economic significance and sustainability challenges.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as allowing access to graphic organisers to summarise the impacts of primary industries.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Primary production. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Planet Earth

The focus area Primary production draws on Planet Earth for foundational knowledge of geomorphic processes, climate patterns and ecosystems that influence agricultural, forestry, fishing and mining activities.

  • Global citizenship

The content in Global citizenship provides a lens through which to evaluate the sustainability, equity and global consequences of primary production systems, including ethical food sourcing and environmental stewardship.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Geographical inquiry is a component of Thinking and working geographically which deepens students’ geographical understanding. The stages of a complete geographical inquiry include:

Geographical inquiry skills are to be integrated with syllabus content and explicitly taught. The focus areas provide a context for developing and applying these inquiry skills. Inquiries may vary in scale and geographical context, involving students in geographical investigations that occur in class or through fieldwork. Communicating the findings of a geographical inquiry can take many forms and should consider the age and stage of learning as well as provide a way that is meaningful and appropriate for a student to convey information.

Students may undertake a complete inquiry process or parts of the inquiry process. Inquiry can be done as a class, in small groups or individually.

Teachers are encouraged to:

  • guide students to develop geographical questions using their senses to observe what is around them and gain insights into their surroundings
  • explicitly teach students to use a range of geographical tools
  • guide students to identify and interpret data
  • provide scaffolds and prompts to assist students to investigate and reflect on findings
  • provide examples of questions to ask about different places, such as ‘What do people do here?’
  • support the use of graphics or audio to communicate students’ findings
  • support students’ engagement through community participation.

Students communicate data, findings and ideas using relevant geographical terms and concepts.

Students may be provided with data to represent a geographical inquiry rather than students collecting information themselves, to facilitate opportunities for participation and inclusion for all students.

Questions for geographical inquiry could include:

  • What is it?
  • Where is it?
  • Why is it there?
  • What are the impacts of it being there?
  • How is it changing over time?
  • Why is it changing?
  • Should anything be done about it?
  • What action might be appropriate?
  • What might it be like in the future?

Suggested geographical inquiry questions are outlined in the teaching advice for each focus area. Schools have the flexibility to select and adapt questions to suit their students’ learning needs.

  • Planet Earth
  • Extreme environments
  • Oceanography
  • Interactions and patterns across a continent
  • Global citizenship
  • Geopolitics
  • Australia’s neighbours
  • Primary production

Geographical tools are an essential component of Thinking and working geographically.

Teachers guide students to develop an understanding of the purpose of specific tools and how they can be used as part of geographical inquiry. Teachers can select appropriate tools to conduct a geographical inquiry based on students’ needs, interests and abilities, and should ensure accessibility for all students.

Students with disability may require adjustments to access geographical tools, for example:

  • tactile maps to investigate landforms and features
  • high contrast maps
  • clear and concise instructions
  • accessible images with alt text, accessible infographics, audio, or high-contrast graphs
  • assistive technologies such as screen readers to access geographical information
  • video recording or audio recording equipment to capture soundscape
  • use of a range of formats such as visual, written or multimodal
  • augmentative and alternative communication to communicate geographical information.

It is important for teachers to provide examples of geographical tools for students and explicitly model how geographical tools are best selected and can be used to support geographical inquiry.

Further advice about Geographical tools is provided in the teaching advice for each focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

When students explore the physical and human features of countries, they develop an understanding of the factors that determine where people live. Learning about the countries in the Asia-Pacific region helps students to recognise the interrelationships between neighbouring countries, such as culture and resources. Students develop an appreciation of the diversity of our world.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching about countries of the Asia-Pacific region, the outcome requires students to recognise places and environments. Students recognise images of a range of places in the Asia-Pacific region, such as Mount Fuji, the Great Wall of China or the Great Barrier Reef.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Place – places are important to people for various reasons, including cultural and economic factors.
  • Interconnection – relationships between people and places in the Asia-Pacific region are influenced by various factors, including migration, travel and trade.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale maps and small-scale maps, political maps, thematic maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsColumn graphs, line graphs, bar graphs, sector graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite imagesMultimedia, mind maps, cartoons

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Examples of fieldwork could include conducting interviews with people from countries in the Asia-Pacific region to explore diverse celebrations, food, religion or traditions.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

  • What kinds of landforms, such as mountains, reefs and islands, are found in the Asia-Pacific region?
  • How does climate vary from Australia to Asia to the Pacific Islands? Select a country in each region to compare.
  • Why is it important to know about the land and weather in this region?

Investigative study

Through the investigative study, students have the opportunity to explore ONE country in the Asia-Pacific region.

For example, students may explore how climate change is affecting Fiji through rising sea levels and increased extreme weather events. They can explore the roles and responses of individuals, groups and governments in enhancing disaster resilience in Fiji, such as the work of Pacific Women Lead (PWL) and government responses, such as relocation of communities affected by rising sea levels.

Connecting with Stage 5 Geography Elective

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography Elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Influence of cultural diversity within the Asia-Pacific region on Australian identity and society
The teacher provides students with examples of cultural diversity that have made an impact on Australia’s identity, such as the Lunar New Year celebrations, Ramadan night street food markets or Diwali celebrations.

Students investigate the cultural traditions of a chosen country in the Asia-Pacific region and assess the impact that country has made on Australia’s identity. Students present their findings as a podcast, video or written response.

Life Skills

  • Cultures of the Asia-Pacific region represented in Australia, including through celebrations, food, religion and traditions
The teacher provides students with examples of cultural diversity that have made an impact on Australia’s identity, such as the Lunar New Year celebrations, Ramadan night street food markets or Diwali celebrations.

Students explore the cultural traditions of a chosen country in the Asia-Pacific region that has made an impact on Australia’s identity. Students are supported to present their findings through an oral, written or multimodal response on how this culture has made an impact on Australia’s identity.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

By investigating global politics, students explore how individuals, groups, governments and international organisations respond to global challenges. Through learning about different political systems, global cooperation and the causes of conflict, students develop an understanding of how countries work together for positive change.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching the reasons individuals or groups might experience conflict, the outcome requires students to identify how individuals and groups can respond to geographical issues. Students are presented with a conflict between countries and match individuals, groups or governments involved with possible responses.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Interconnection – relationships between people, places and environments impact how individuals and groups respond to geographical issues.
  • Scale – individuals, organisations and governments can work together to provide aid or assistance to countries experiencing conflict, natural disasters or environmental events.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, political maps, thematic mapsClimate graphsVirtual or digital maps, augmented reality and virtual realityAboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Knowledge Systems (such as Cultural mapping and Oral histories), infographics, mind maps, cartoons, flow charts, digital tools (such as apps and web tools)

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Examples of fieldwork could include:

  • conducting a field visit, in-person or virtually, to a local cultural centre, restaurant, shop, port or embassy to observe and record data about how individuals, groups or governments are responding to Australia’s position on climate change. Students may use fieldwork tools, such as observational checklists, interviews or photographs, to gather data.
  • designing and conducting interviews or questionnaires with members of the school community, local organisations or family members to identify similarities or differences in perspectives on a current geopolitical issue.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

  • When can different perspectives lead to conflict?
  • Why do countries sometimes fight over land or sea areas?
  • How does a country’s location and natural features affect its power (e.g. trade and resources)?

Investigative study

Through the investigative study, students have the opportunity to explore ONE area of political tension or conflict. For example:

  • Australia’s involvement in international peacekeeping efforts and humanitarian missions
  • Australia’s participation in global responses to international security challenges
  • Australia’s engagement in international climate change agreements and environmental diplomacy.

Connecting with Stage 5 Geography Elective

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography Elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Role of international organisations in facilitating trade, promoting development and maintaining international cooperation
The teacher selects an issue faced by international organisations that suits the interests of students, such as climate change. Students break into small groups to represent different people and organisations that will influence the issue, such as the United Nations, governments, businesses or activists.

Students develop a scenario to explain the perspectives of the people or organisations they represent and influence an agreement that suits all stakeholders involved.

Life Skills

  • Role of the United Nations in promoting cooperation between countries
The teacher selects an issue faced by international organisations that suits the interests of students, such as climate change. The teacher explains that the role of the United Nations is similar to the role of the school representative council, and its role is to help groups of people with different ideas come together to solve problems.

Students are assigned the role of a United Nations activist. Students identify the United Nations perspective on the issue presented in their group’s scenario.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

By learning about global citizenship, students can explore their responsibilities and those of other individuals, communities and governments in responding to environmental, social or economic challenges. Students consider what it means to be a responsible national and global citizen and how their own actions can contribute to positive change.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching about global geographic challenges, the outcome requires the students to examine geographical issues or events. Students inquire into how unethical mining impacts the environment.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Interconnection – people, places and environments are interconnected.
  • Scale – a range of geographical issues affect global citizens and these can be managed at a local, national or global level.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, political maps, thematic mapsColumn graphs, line graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, global positioning systems (GPS), virtual realityIllustrations, infographics, cartoons, flow charts

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Examples of fieldwork could include a virtual or in-person visit to environments impacted by rising sea levels.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

  • What is the nature of the global issue?
  • Why has the issue occurred?
  • How have individuals, governments and organisations assisted with the issue?

Investigative study

Through the investigative study, students have the opportunity to explore ONE environmental, social or economic challenge. For example:

  • Environmental – how the shopping habits of Australians impact environments in other countries.
  • Social – Australia’s collaboration with the World Health Organization (WHO) in response to global health issues, such as pandemics.
  • Economic – the role of Australian aid organisations in providing financial relief to other countries.

Connecting with Stage 5 Geography Elective

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography Elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Nature of challenges such as climate change, conflicts, public health crises and tensions in global politics that require international cooperation

The teacher divides the class into groups and assigns each group a global challenge, such as:

  • climate change
  • conflicts
  • public health crises
  • tensions in global politics.

In small groups, students analyse their global challenge by responding to guiding questions, such as:

  • What is the issue?
  • Who is helping?
  • How can we help?

Students represent the responses of individuals, groups or governments to the global challenge through their choice of a multimodal presentation, drama skit or visual poster.

Life Skills

  • Global geographic challenges in the world today

The teacher divides the class into groups and assigns each group a global challenge, such as:

  • climate change
  • conflicts
  • public health crises.

The teacher provides a scaffold with sentence starters to support students to identify how individuals and groups are responding to the geographical issue. Students should be allocated roles within their team.

In their groups, students create a presentation on how individuals and groups are responding to their assigned global challenge, and share it with the class.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

This option provides schools with the opportunity to develop students’ geographical knowledge and understanding of a particular location and/or area of inquiry that caters for their needs and interests. This study also provides an opportunity to investigate a geographical issue in depth and to undertake fieldwork in the local area or at an accessible location. Students use geographical inquiry skills to investigate the interactions between people and environments and the civics and citizenship aspects of a selected study.

Planning a school-developed option

When planning a school-developed option teachers should consider:

  • focusing on ONE specific area of interest that builds on prior knowledge or addresses either physical geography or human geography or a combination of both
  • working with local Aboriginal Communities to ensure effective and respectful planning and teaching of Cultural Knowledges and Practices with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.

The following process may be helpful when planning for teaching and learning of this focus area.

Image long description: Six steps when planning for teaching and learning appear in individual boxes as a flow chart. Arrows pointing from left to right appear between each box. The steps are ordered: Select an area of interest; Determine the focus of study; Consider geographical concepts; Consider geographical inquiry skills; Consider geographical tools; and Teach content.

Suggested areas of interest and focus of study

The school-developed option should provide students with opportunities to learn about a specific area of interest in the field of geography. The following table contains suggestions for this.

Area of interestFocus of study
Aboriginal land managementCaring for Country – traditional Knowledges and sustainable land use
Active citizenship investigating local environmental issues and community responsesLocal environmental action – people protecting places and environments
Coastal erosion and managementBeaches at risk – protecting shorelines from erosion
Cultural landscapes and heritage sitesStories in the landscape – the geography of heritage and identity
Deforestation and land cover changeVanishing forests – tracking land cover change over time
Geography of health and diseaseMapping health – how geography influences disease and wellbeing
Impacts of climate change on the local areaWeather and place – how climate change is reshaping local environments
Local waterways and catchment managementRivers, lakes and creeks – change and management
Renewable energy and sustainabilityPowering the future – the transition to renewable energy in local communities
Smart cities and sustainable urban developmentCities of the future – how technology is shaping urban spaces
Transport networks and urban planningGetting around – transport, traffic and the changing city landscape
Urban and regional planning processesPlanning our places – how decisions shape land use, infrastructure and liveability
Urban heat islands creating environmental changeHot cities, cool solutions – the fight against urban heat islands
Urban sprawl and its impactsGrowing cities, loss of greenfield sites – the cost of urban sprawl
Waste management and recyclingRethinking waste – the journey from rubbish to resource

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be addressed, if appropriate.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Geographical inquiry skills

Geographical inquiry skills can be integrated into teaching and learning activities. Teachers can develop key inquiry questions to guide and support the application of inquiry skills.

Connecting with Stage 5

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content integrated with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography elective in Stage 4.

When selecting an option, consider one that engages all students. For example, when engaging with a school-developed option about a suburb-specific site study, students studying Life Skills content could create a suburb profile in their preferred form, such as a:

  • poster or multimodal presentation including maps and images
  • 3D model using recycled materials
  • podcast interviewing a local planner or councillor.

Students studying Stage 5 content could design a campaign to manage and protect the local environment.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

By learning about extreme environments, students develop an understanding of the characteristics of various environments and recognise how to stay safe in extreme environmental events. They develop an awareness of the impact extreme environments have on people and places. They build skills to respond to environmental issues that affect their lives as active global citizens.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching ways to stay safe in extreme environmental events, the outcome requires students to identify human activity in a range of environments. Students could identify clothing and equipment required to live in an extreme environment, such as the subarctic climate of Lapland.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, tools and inquiry skills can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Sustainability – the ability of environments to support life depends on how they are cared for, including reducing the impact of human activities.
  • Change – the environment changes over time due to natural processes, such as tectonic activity, glaciation and wind action. Human interactions, such as reducing water usage and resource usage, can protect extreme environments.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale and small-scale maps, physical maps, thematic maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsColumn graphs, line graphs, bar graphs, sector graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, geographic information systems (GIS), augmented reality and virtual realityIllustrations, multimedia, diagrams, infographics, digital tools (such as apps and web tools), photographs by location

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

An example of fieldwork could include exploring a virtual tour of the Svalbard Global Seed Vault in Norway to investigate the facility and the safety measures used by scientists, including specialised clothing.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

  • What are the characteristics and features of the extreme environment?
  • Why do humans face challenges when living in or visiting this extreme environment?
  • What would I need to stay safe and survive in this extreme environment?

Investigative study

Through the investigative study, students have the opportunity to explore ONE extreme environment. For example:

  • Deserts – The Great Sandy Desert (Australia)
  • High altitudes – Himalayas (China, Bhutan, Nepal, India and Pakistan)
  • Polar regions – Antarctica
  • Volcanoes – Mount Etna (Italy).

Geographical issues that may be examined in relation to the selected environment include deforestation, climate change, loss of biodiversity, water scarcity, waste and pollution.

Connecting with Stage 5 Geography Elective

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography Elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Global distribution of extreme environments including high-altitude areas, polar regions, deserts, geothermal zones
The teacher identifies examples of extreme environments across the globe and demonstrates how to record location data, such as continent and latitude.

Students use a variety of maps, including digital maps or tactile graphics or models, to plot the locations of extreme environments and categorise them by continent and environment type, such as polar, desert, mountain.

Using the mapped data, students create a table or graph to compare the different types of extreme environments by continent.

Life Skills

  • Locations of extreme environments
The teacher provides students with a list of extreme environments around the world. The teacher supports students to locate these environments and record them on a physical, digital or a tactile map.

The teacher asks the inquiry question, ‘Why are many extreme environments located close to the equator or far away from the equator?’

title.name: 📜 Title
title.value: Teaching advice for Life Skills Physical geography: Extreme environments

system.name: LS S4/S5 Teaching advice for Life Skills Physical geography: Extreme environments

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Purpose

By investigating ONE transect, students explore the diverse physical environments, natural resources and human activities found along its path. Learning about human activities and significant events and issues along the selected transect helps students to understand the connections between people, places and environments, and the impacts of these interactions. Students learn to sustainably manage and protect land and water resources along the transect.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching the management or protection of natural resources along the selected transect, the outcome requires students to identify features or characteristics of places and environments. Students could identify images or objects that represent protected natural resources in a local area transect.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Space – spatial patterns along a transect, including the distribution of landforms, resources and human activities.
  • Change – landscapes, landforms and environments change over time due to natural processes (e.g. weathering, erosion and deposition) and human influences (e.g. settlement and land use).

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale and small-scale maps, topographic maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsColumn graphs, line graphs, bar graphs, sector graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images3D models and globes, illustrations, tactile graphics and models, paintings and artworks, sketches (such as field sketches, line drawings and photo sketches), photographs by location

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Examples of fieldwork could include exploring transects in the local area, such as between home and school.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

content.value:
Purpose

By learning about the features and characteristics of oceans, students understand the importance of protecting them. By reflecting on recreational, cultural and commercial interactions with oceans, students can develop an awareness of how individuals and groups can take responsibility for protecting and managing marine environments.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching ways to keep oceans clean, the outcome requires students to demonstrate ways to manage and protect a place or environment. Students could use a checklist to demonstrate the different ways people can keep oceans clean.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, tools and inquiry skills can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Interconnection – oceans connect people, places and environments through ocean currents, marine biodiversity, trade routes and climate regulation.
  • Change – changes to natural processes, such as movement of water and transfer of heat, can impact sea levels and marine ecosystems. Human interactions, such as release of waste, pollution, overfishing or tourism, can impact oceans.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, physical mapsColumn graphs, line graphs, bar graphs, sector graphsVirtual or digital maps, augmented reality and virtual reality3D models and globes, tactile graphics and models, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Knowledge Systems (such as Cultural mapping and Oral histories), diagrams, flow charts, digital tools (such as apps and web tools)

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Examples of fieldwork could include:

  • a virtual tour of Australia’s Great Barrier Reef using websites, documentaries or virtual reality experiences to recognise how the reef has changed over time
  • on-Country experiences with traditional Custodians to learn about the customs, Cultures and connections Aboriginal Peoples have to saltwater Country.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

  • What are the major oceans around the world and where are they located?
  • How do people from a variety of cultures use the ocean?
  • Why is it important to be responsible users of the oceans?

Investigative study

Through the investigative study, students have the opportunity to explore ONE issue relating to the use of oceans.

Examples of issues that could be investigated include:

  • environmental impacts affecting oceans around the world (e.g. coral bleaching and water temperatures rising on the Great Barrier Reef)
  • how people can minimise their impact on the ocean (e.g. reducing use of plastics, participating in beach clean-ups).

Connecting with Stage 5 Geography Elective

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography Elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • Economic, cultural and recreational value of the world’s oceans
The teacher facilitates a brainstorming session on how people around the world use oceans. In small groups or individually, students create an infographic analysing economic, cultural and recreational activities across the world’s oceans. The teacher models features of effective infographics.

Life Skills

  • How the ocean is used for commercial purposes
The teacher facilitates a brainstorming session on how people around the world use oceans, specifically using the prompt question: ‘Which industries rely on the ocean?’

In small groups or individually, students create an infographic or poster identifying how the ocean is used by humans for commercial purposes. The teacher provides students with a model and a template to guide the creation of the infographic.

Purpose

Learning about Earth supports students’ understanding of the world around them. Students develop awareness of how to interact with environments by exploring natural features, weather and climate. Learning about plants and animals in different environments helps students recognise the importance of caring for the environment.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching geomorphic features of Earth, the outcome requires students to identify features or characteristics of places and environments. Students match labels to images of features, such as coastline, cliffs, caves, rivers, mountains or beaches.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Environment – environments have a range of features, including physical features, climate and weather patterns, and plants and animals.
  • Change – the Earth is changing due to natural processes and human interactions. Natural processes include weathering, erosion, deposition, tectonic plate movement and natural hazards.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale and small-scale maps, physical maps, topographic and thematic maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsPicture graphs, column graphs, line graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, global positioning systems (GPS), geographic information systems (GIS), virtual reality3D models and globes, illustrations, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Knowledge Systems (such as Cultural mapping and Oral histories), paintings and artworks, diagrams, mind maps, flow charts, sketches (such as field sketches, line drawings and photo sketches), photographs by location

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Examples of fieldwork could include:

  • a visit to a local waterway to observe vegetation and bank stability
  • on-Country experiences with traditional Custodians to learn about the interactions of Aboriginal Peoples in local environments.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

  • What are some of the features of plants and animals that help them adapt to the environment?
  • Why do humans need to practise sensitivity when interacting with ecological wonders?
  • How can people stay safe when interacting with the environment?

Investigative study

Through the investigative study, students have the opportunity to explore ONE environment.

For example, students may explore the caves and grottoes of Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng in Vietnam and its ecosystems. This could include a study of the Phong Nha stick insect and cave gecko, which are not found anywhere else on Earth, and endangered species such as the Indochinese tiger and Asian black bear.

Connecting with Stage 5 Geography Elective

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography Elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • The associated roles of water, wind and ice in the processes of weathering, erosion and deposition responsible for transforming the Earth’s surface
The teacher uses geographical tools to show students evidence of the effects of water, wind and ice in different environments.

Students engage with tools to analyse weathering, erosion and deposition processes. They create a written text or multimodal presentation to analyse the role of water, wind or ice in transforming the environment.

Life Skills

  • Changes in landscape features as a result of weathering, erosion or deposition
The teacher uses geographical tools to show students evidence of the effects of water, wind and ice in different environments.

The teacher models deposition by using a fan to blow loose material, such as sand, from a surface. Students describe how the wind has moved the sand to a new location and changed the features of the simulated landscape.

Geographical inquiry is a component of Thinking and working geographically which deepens students’ geographical understanding. The stages of a complete geographical inquiry include:

Geographical inquiry skills are to be integrated with syllabus content and explicitly taught. The focus areas provide a context for developing and applying these inquiry skills. Inquiries may vary in scale and geographical context, involving students in geographical investigations that occur in class or through fieldwork.

Teachers are encouraged to:

  • guide students to develop geographical questions, using their senses to observe what is around them and gain insights into their surroundings, supporting students to understand their environment and gather data
  • explicitly teach students to analyse and use a range of geographical tools to represent data including observing patterns and relationships, and drawing conclusions
  • guide students to develop their creative thinking skills to synthesise data and represent findings and ideas
  • provide scaffolds and prompts to assist students to reflect on and evaluate findings
  • support students’ engagement in active citizenship, such as community participation, while using critical thinking skills to solve problems.

Students communicate data, findings and ideas using relevant geographical terms and concepts.

Important questions for geographical inquiry could include:

  • What is it?
  • Where is it?
  • Why is it there?
  • What are the impacts of it being there?
  • How is it changing over time?
  • Why is it changing?
  • Should anything be done about it?
  • What action might be appropriate?
  • What might it be like in the future?

Suggested geographical inquiry questions are outlined in the teaching advice for each focus area. Schools have the flexibility to select and adapt questions to suit their students’ learning needs. Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the physical, cultural and economic geography of the Asia-Pacific region. They learn about the diversity of physical environments and how geomorphic and atmospheric processes influence human settlement, access to resources and environmental challenges. Students examine the cultural and historical factors that shape societies across the region, and how demographic, urban and settlement patterns vary between countries. They investigate spatial variations in development, patterns of production and trade, and the economic interdependence between countries in the Asia-Pacific region. Students also consider the role of regional organisations in addressing shared challenges.

Key terms

  • atmospheric processes
  • contemporary geographical issue
  • economic interdependence
  • environmental challenges
  • geomorphic

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Place: The diverse physical and cultural characteristics of countries in the Asia-Pacific region, including variations in landforms, climate, population and cultural identity, and how these influence patterns of human settlement and development.
  • Interconnection: The economic, social and political connections between Australia and its regional neighbours, including trade relationships, migration, development cooperation and shared responses to environmental and social challenges.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How do physical environments and natural processes shape the diversity of landscapes and settlement patterns in the Asia-Pacific region?
  • How do cultural and historical influences shape the identities and settlement patterns of countries in the Asia-Pacific region?
  • What economic patterns and trade connections exist across the Asia-Pacific region, and how do they contribute to regional interdependence?
  • What are the key geographical issues affecting countries in the Asia-Pacific region, and how are different groups responding to these challenges?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Australia’s neighbours content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale maps and small-scale maps, relief maps, political maps, land use maps, isoline maps, cartogram maps, dot maps, flowline maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsPopulation profiles, scatter plots, bubble charts, line graphs, column graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, remote sensing dataMultimedia, mind maps, cartoons, transects

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as accessing pre-prepared checklists or identification tables to catalogue the diversity of physical environments in the Asia-Pacific region.
  • Encouraging empathy and intercultural understanding by promoting respectful engagement with diverse perspectives and valuing the lived experiences of people in neighbouring countries.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Australia’s neighbours. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Interactions and patterns across a continent

The focus area Australia’s neighbours builds on the study of spatial and cultural diversity examined in Interactions and patterns across a continent and reinforces understanding of environmental influences on settlement and development.

  • Geopolitics

The content of Australia’s neighbours supports and is supported by Geopolitics through shared themes of regional cooperation, political relationships, development and migration patterns.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the geopolitical characteristics of the world, including political systems, sovereignty and the spatial patterns of political affiliation. They learn how political, economic and military powers influence international relations, governance and cooperation. Students examine causes and consequences of political tension and conflict as well as the roles of individuals, groups and governments in promoting peace, resolving disputes and supporting recovery. They investigate how political systems and international organisations contribute to positive change through diplomacy, development and the promotion of human rights.

Key terms

  • diplomacy
  • international cooperation
  • nation-states
  • peacebuilding
  • political affiliations
  • sovereignty

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Space: The spatial organisation and distribution of political systems, power, boundaries and affiliations at local, national and global scales, and how these influence governance, conflict and diplomacy.
  • Environment: The role of global and regional political systems in addressing environmental challenges, managing natural resources and supporting sustainability through cooperation, treaties and international agreements.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How do political systems, nation-states and sovereignty shape global political boundaries and international relations?
  • What factors cause political tension and conflict, and how can they be managed or resolved at different scales?
  • How do international organisations and diplomatic efforts contribute to peacebuilding, development and cooperation?
  • How are global challenges such as environmental sustainability and human rights being addressed through political cooperation and agreements?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Geopolitics content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, political maps, choropleth maps, cartogram maps, dot maps, flowline maps, graduated or proportional symbol mapsClimate graphs, population profiles, bubble chartsVirtual or digital maps, augmented reality, virtual reality, remote sensing dataInfographics, mind maps, cartoons, flow charts, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Knowledge Systems, digital tools

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials that explore political systems, territorial disputes, conflict and cooperation between nations and spatial patterns of political attitudes or voting behaviours.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as building background knowledge before engaging with case study materials.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.
  • Drawing students’ attention to the representations of some places on maps, such as borders and place names, and how they may be contested by particular communities.
  • Encouraging critical thinking when examining diverse perspectives.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Geopolitics. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Extreme environments

The presence of extreme environments can intensify geopolitical tensions due to competition over resources, territorial claims or challenges related to migration and humanitarian access.

  • Australia’s neighbours

The focus area Australia’s neighbours helps contextualise geopolitical relationships in the Asia-Pacific region, including the influence of political systems, regional cooperation and strategic alliances.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the values and attitudes that underpin global citizenship. They learn about the interdependence of the global economy, the environment and society, and how global challenges such as climate change, inequality and conflict require collective action and international cooperation. Students examine how technology and global connectivity shape global citizenship and how ethical responsibilities influence decisions and actions across a range of scales. Through case studies of global citizenship in action, students investigate initiatives that promote human rights, sustainability and equity, including the contributions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and other international Indigenous Peoples.

  • advocacy
  • environmental stewardship
  • global citizenship
  • global connectivity
  • globalisation
  • intergovernmental organisations

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Interconnection: The interdependence of countries, societies and environments through global trade, environmental issues, migration and shared challenges.
  • Sustainability: The role of global citizens in contributing to sustainable futures by addressing climate change, inequality and responsible resource use.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • What values and attitudes define global citizenship?
  • How do global, economic, environmental and social interdependencies create challenges that require collaborative solutions?
  • In what ways do technologies influence global connectivity and the concept of global citizenship?
  • How can individuals and communities engage in global citizenship to address environmental, social and economic issues?

Geographical tools

Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials that explore global interconnections, cultural diversity, international cooperation and shared responsibilities in addressing global challenges such as climate change, inequality or migration.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the global distribution and environmental conditions of extreme environments. They learn how factors such as climate, altitude, terrain and chemical composition contribute to environmental extremes and influence the survival of living organisms. Students examine the role of atmospheric, geomorphic and geophysical processes in shaping extreme environments. They also examine how climate change can intensify and expand the severity and extent of extreme environments and cause other environments to become more prone to extreme events. The significance of Indigenous Knowledges in managing extreme environments and addressing other contemporary geographical issues is also addressed.

Key terms

  • extreme environmental events
  • extreme environments
  • geomorphic
  • geophysical

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Place: The distinctive characteristics of extreme environments, including climate, terrain and chemical conditions, and how these affect the habitability and significance of specific places.
  • Change: The intensification of environmental extremes over time due to climatic, physical and human processes, including the role of climate change in reshaping these environments.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • What makes an environment extreme and how do environmental extremes differ from extreme environmental events?
  • How do climate, altitude and geophysical processes contribute to the formation and intensification of extreme environments?
  • How do living things, including humans, adapt to survive in extreme environments?
  • What challenges do extreme environments present for human habitation and how are these challenges being managed and overcome?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Extreme environments content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the physical geography focus areas should enable students to meaningfully investigate natural processes and features in accessible local environments. Where direct observation is not possible, students should investigate how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. In the case of large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, students may access digital technologies to undertake fieldwork and to provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials from a range of extreme environments, such as polar, desert, high-altitude and geothermal regions, to highlight the physical challenges, environmental processes and human adaptations specific to each setting.

  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.
  • Drawing students’ attention to the ecocentric world views of Aboriginal Peoples and other international Indigenous Peoples to highlight reciprocal relationships with extreme environments grounded in custodianship and sustainability.
