Purpose

Learning about Earth supports students’ understanding of the world around them. Students develop awareness of how to interact with environments by exploring natural features, weather and climate. Learning about plants and animals in different environments helps students recognise the importance of caring for the environment.

Considerations for teaching and learning

Outcomes and content

Outcomes determine the scope of learning for the selected content points. For example, when teaching geomorphic features of Earth, the outcome requires students to identify features or characteristics of places and environments. Students match labels to images of features, such as coastline, cliffs, caves, rivers, mountains or beaches.

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into the focus area.

Geographical concepts

One or more geographical concepts can be integrated into this focus area. For example:

  • Environment – environments have a range of features, including physical features, climate and weather patterns, and plants and animals.
  • Change – the Earth is changing due to natural processes and human interactions. Natural processes include weathering, erosion, deposition, tectonic plate movement and natural hazards.

Geographical tools

Geographical tools should suit the content, individual student learning needs and the school context.

Examples of tools:

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale and small-scale maps, physical maps, topographic and thematic maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsPicture graphs, column graphs, line graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, global positioning systems (GPS), geographic information systems (GIS), virtual reality3D models and globes, illustrations, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Knowledge Systems (such as Cultural mapping and Oral histories), paintings and artworks, diagrams, mind maps, flow charts, sketches (such as field sketches, line drawings and photo sketches), photographs by location

Fieldwork provides opportunities for students to participate in geographical inquiry at school, offsite or virtually. Selected environments and locations should be accessible to all students.

Examples of fieldwork could include:

  • a visit to a local waterway to observe vegetation and bank stability
  • on-Country experiences with traditional Custodians to learn about the interactions of Aboriginal Peoples in local environments.

Geographical inquiry

Inquiry questions can guide and support the application of inquiry skills. For example:

  • What are some of the features of plants and animals that help them adapt to the environment?
  • Why do humans need to practise sensitivity when interacting with ecological wonders?
  • How can people stay safe when interacting with the environment?

Investigative study

Through the investigative study, students have the opportunity to explore ONE environment.

For example, students may explore the caves and grottoes of Phong Nha-Kẻ Bàng in Vietnam and its ecosystems. This could include a study of the Phong Nha stick insect and cave gecko, which are not found anywhere else on Earth, and endangered species such as the Indochinese tiger and Asian black bear.

Connecting with Stage 5 Geography Elective

Teachers may be programming Life Skills content by integrating it with Stage 5 content to meet the needs of students accessing different outcomes in the same class. A student cannot study Life Skills outcomes in combination with Stage 5 Geography Elective outcomes, or any outcomes determined for delivery of Geography in Stage 4.

Below is an example of how the Life Skills syllabus content for this focus area can be taught with the Stage 5 syllabus content.

Syllabus contentSuggested teaching and learning activities

Stage 5

  • The associated roles of water, wind and ice in the processes of weathering, erosion and deposition responsible for transforming the Earth’s surface
The teacher uses geographical tools to show students evidence of the effects of water, wind and ice in different environments.

Students engage with tools to analyse weathering, erosion and deposition processes. They create a written text or multimodal presentation to analyse the role of water, wind or ice in transforming the environment.

Life Skills

  • Changes in landscape features as a result of weathering, erosion or deposition
The teacher uses geographical tools to show students evidence of the effects of water, wind and ice in different environments.

The teacher models deposition by using a fan to blow loose material, such as sand, from a surface. Students describe how the wind has moved the sand to a new location and changed the features of the simulated landscape.

Geographical inquiry is a component of Thinking and working geographically which deepens students’ geographical understanding. The stages of a complete geographical inquiry include:

Geographical inquiry skills are to be integrated with syllabus content and explicitly taught. The focus areas provide a context for developing and applying these inquiry skills. Inquiries may vary in scale and geographical context, involving students in geographical investigations that occur in class or through fieldwork.

Teachers are encouraged to:

  • guide students to develop geographical questions, using their senses to observe what is around them and gain insights into their surroundings, supporting students to understand their environment and gather data
  • explicitly teach students to analyse and use a range of geographical tools to represent data including observing patterns and relationships, and drawing conclusions
  • guide students to develop their creative thinking skills to synthesise data and represent findings and ideas
  • provide scaffolds and prompts to assist students to reflect on and evaluate findings
  • support students’ engagement in active citizenship, such as community participation, while using critical thinking skills to solve problems.

Students communicate data, findings and ideas using relevant geographical terms and concepts.

Important questions for geographical inquiry could include:

  • What is it?
  • Where is it?
  • Why is it there?
  • What are the impacts of it being there?
  • How is it changing over time?
  • Why is it changing?
  • Should anything be done about it?
  • What action might be appropriate?
  • What might it be like in the future?

Suggested geographical inquiry questions are outlined in the teaching advice for each focus area. Schools have the flexibility to select and adapt questions to suit their students’ learning needs. Key inquiry questions can be used to check for understanding and cover the breadth of each focus area.

content.name: 📜 Content
content.value:
Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the physical, cultural and economic geography of the Asia-Pacific region. They learn about the diversity of physical environments and how geomorphic and atmospheric processes influence human settlement, access to resources and environmental challenges. Students examine the cultural and historical factors that shape societies across the region, and how demographic, urban and settlement patterns vary between countries. They investigate spatial variations in development, patterns of production and trade, and the economic interdependence between countries in the Asia-Pacific region. Students also consider the role of regional organisations in addressing shared challenges.

Key terms

  • atmospheric processes
  • contemporary geographical issue
  • economic interdependence
  • environmental challenges
  • geomorphic

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Place: The diverse physical and cultural characteristics of countries in the Asia-Pacific region, including variations in landforms, climate, population and cultural identity, and how these influence patterns of human settlement and development.
  • Interconnection: The economic, social and political connections between Australia and its regional neighbours, including trade relationships, migration, development cooperation and shared responses to environmental and social challenges.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How do physical environments and natural processes shape the diversity of landscapes and settlement patterns in the Asia-Pacific region?
  • How do cultural and historical influences shape the identities and settlement patterns of countries in the Asia-Pacific region?
  • What economic patterns and trade connections exist across the Asia-Pacific region, and how do they contribute to regional interdependence?
  • What are the key geographical issues affecting countries in the Asia-Pacific region, and how are different groups responding to these challenges?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Australia’s neighbours content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale maps and small-scale maps, relief maps, political maps, land use maps, isoline maps, cartogram maps, dot maps, flowline maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsPopulation profiles, scatter plots, bubble charts, line graphs, column graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, remote sensing dataMultimedia, mind maps, cartoons, transects

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as accessing pre-prepared checklists or identification tables to catalogue the diversity of physical environments in the Asia-Pacific region.
  • Encouraging empathy and intercultural understanding by promoting respectful engagement with diverse perspectives and valuing the lived experiences of people in neighbouring countries.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Australia’s neighbours. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Interactions and patterns across a continent

The focus area Australia’s neighbours builds on the study of spatial and cultural diversity examined in Interactions and patterns across a continent and reinforces understanding of environmental influences on settlement and development.

  • Geopolitics

The content of Australia’s neighbours supports and is supported by Geopolitics through shared themes of regional cooperation, political relationships, development and migration patterns.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the geopolitical characteristics of the world, including political systems, sovereignty and the spatial patterns of political affiliation. They learn how political, economic and military powers influence international relations, governance and cooperation. Students examine causes and consequences of political tension and conflict as well as the roles of individuals, groups and governments in promoting peace, resolving disputes and supporting recovery. They investigate how political systems and international organisations contribute to positive change through diplomacy, development and the promotion of human rights.

Key terms

  • diplomacy
  • international cooperation
  • nation-states
  • peacebuilding
  • political affiliations
  • sovereignty

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Space: The spatial organisation and distribution of political systems, power, boundaries and affiliations at local, national and global scales, and how these influence governance, conflict and diplomacy.
  • Environment: The role of global and regional political systems in addressing environmental challenges, managing natural resources and supporting sustainability through cooperation, treaties and international agreements.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How do political systems, nation-states and sovereignty shape global political boundaries and international relations?
  • What factors cause political tension and conflict, and how can they be managed or resolved at different scales?
  • How do international organisations and diplomatic efforts contribute to peacebuilding, development and cooperation?
  • How are global challenges such as environmental sustainability and human rights being addressed through political cooperation and agreements?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Geopolitics content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, political maps, choropleth maps, cartogram maps, dot maps, flowline maps, graduated or proportional symbol mapsClimate graphs, population profiles, bubble chartsVirtual or digital maps, augmented reality, virtual reality, remote sensing dataInfographics, mind maps, cartoons, flow charts, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Knowledge Systems, digital tools

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials that explore political systems, territorial disputes, conflict and cooperation between nations and spatial patterns of political attitudes or voting behaviours.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as building background knowledge before engaging with case study materials.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.
  • Drawing students’ attention to the representations of some places on maps, such as borders and place names, and how they may be contested by particular communities.
  • Encouraging critical thinking when examining diverse perspectives.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Geopolitics. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Extreme environments

The presence of extreme environments can intensify geopolitical tensions due to competition over resources, territorial claims or challenges related to migration and humanitarian access.

  • Australia’s neighbours

The focus area Australia’s neighbours helps contextualise geopolitical relationships in the Asia-Pacific region, including the influence of political systems, regional cooperation and strategic alliances.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the values and attitudes that underpin global citizenship. They learn about the interdependence of the global economy, the environment and society, and how global challenges such as climate change, inequality and conflict require collective action and international cooperation. Students examine how technology and global connectivity shape global citizenship and how ethical responsibilities influence decisions and actions across a range of scales. Through case studies of global citizenship in action, students investigate initiatives that promote human rights, sustainability and equity, including the contributions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and other international Indigenous Peoples.

Key terms

  • advocacy
  • environmental stewardship
  • global citizenship
  • global connectivity
  • globalisation

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the global distribution and environmental conditions of extreme environments. They learn how factors such as climate, altitude, terrain and chemical composition contribute to environmental extremes and influence the survival of living organisms. Students examine the role of atmospheric, geomorphic and geophysical processes in shaping extreme environments. They also examine how climate change can intensify and expand the severity and extent of extreme environments and cause other environments to become more prone to extreme events. The significance of Indigenous Knowledges in managing extreme environments and addressing other contemporary geographical issues is also addressed.

Key terms

  • extreme environmental events
  • extreme environments
  • geomorphic
  • geophysical

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Place: The distinctive characteristics of extreme environments, including climate, terrain and chemical conditions, and how these affect the habitability and significance of specific places.
  • Change: The intensification of environmental extremes over time due to climatic, physical and human processes, including the role of climate change in reshaping these environments.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • What makes an environment extreme and how do environmental extremes differ from extreme environmental events?
  • How do climate, altitude and geophysical processes contribute to the formation and intensification of extreme environments?
  • How do living things, including humans, adapt to survive in extreme environments?
  • What challenges do extreme environments present for human habitation and how are these challenges being managed and overcome?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Extreme environments content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale and small-scale maps, physical maps, précis maps, choropleth maps, weather maps, synoptic chartsSector graphs, scatter plots, line graphs, column graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, geographic information systems (GIS), augmented reality, virtual realityIllustrations, multimedia, diagrams, infographics, digital tools, photographs classified by location and angle

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the physical geography focus areas should enable students to meaningfully investigate natural processes and features in accessible local environments. Where direct observation is not possible, students should investigate how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. In the case of large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, students may access digital technologies to undertake fieldwork and to provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials from a range of extreme environments, such as polar, desert, high-altitude and geothermal regions, to highlight the physical challenges, environmental processes and human adaptations specific to each setting.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as allowing access to audio, visual or multimodal materials for case study investigations.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.
  • Drawing students’ attention to the ecocentric world views of Aboriginal Peoples and other international Indigenous Peoples to highlight reciprocal relationships with extreme environments grounded in custodianship and sustainability.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Extreme environments. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Interactions and patterns across a continent

The focus area Extreme environments supports understanding of how latitude, altitude and atmospheric processes contribute to physical diversity across continental transects.

  • Geopolitics

The physical constraints of extreme environments such as the Arctic, high-altitude zones or desert zones often shape geopolitical dynamics, influencing borders, resource access and strategic significance.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the physical and human geography across a selected transcontinental transect. They learn about the diverse environments along the transect, including variations in vegetation, biodiversity, climate and water resources. Students examine changes in human settlement, cultural diversity and economic activity influenced by the physical environment. They investigate patterns of connectivity through transport networks and the interactions between people and their environments, including land use, natural resource management and the influence of Indigenous Knowledges and Practices. Through studying significant places, events and a contemporary geographical issue, students develop an understanding of environmental change, natural hazards and the future sustainability of the places along the transect.

Key terms

  • biogeographical
  • natural hazards
  • natural resource management
  • settlement patterns
  • sustainable land use practices
  • transect

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Scale: The investigation of physical and human geography across a continental scale, highlighting variations and connections at local, regional and transcontinental levels.
  • Environment: The relationships between physical features, climate, biodiversity and human settlement patterns along the transect and how they shape and are shaped by environmental factors.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How do physical factors such as climate, topography and biodiversity vary along a transcontinental transect?
  • How do population, economic activity and transport networks shape human environments along a transcontinental transect?
  • How do cultural practices, historical events and land use influence human–environment interactions along a transcontinental transect?
  • What environmental challenges and geographical issues emerge along a transcontinental transect and how are they being addressed for future sustainability?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Interactions and patterns across a continent content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale maps, small-scale maps, topographic maps, land use maps, isoline maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsSector graphs, population profiles, line graphs, column graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images3D models and globes, illustrations, tactile graphics and models, paintings and artworks, transects, sketches, photographs classified by location and angle

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the physical geography focus areas should enable students to meaningfully investigate natural processes and features in accessible local environments. Where direct observation is not possible, students should investigate how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. In the case of large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, students may access digital technologies to undertake fieldwork and to provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Guiding students in conducting a transect by supporting them to select, map and interpret data across a linear pathway that reveals changes in the physical and human environment.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as the selection of part of a transcontinental transect.
  • Including a range of case study materials that illustrate variations in physical and human features across a continent, such as changes in landforms, climate zones, population distribution, land use and cultural diversity.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.
  • Providing opportunities for students to connect with Aboriginal Knowledge Holders and/or Elders to share Cultural Knowledges about significant sites located along a relevant transect, for example Perth to Sydney. These Knowledge-sharing opportunities may take place in-person, via email or through videoconferencing.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Interactions and patterns across a continent. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Extreme environments

The focus area Interactions and patterns across a continent provides a framework for exploring physical diversity, including the presence of extreme environments such as deserts, highlands and polar regions.

  • Australia’s neighbours

Understanding spatial and cultural diversity along transects strengthens knowledge of regional characteristics studied in the focus area Australia's neighbours and supports comparative analysis of places.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the spatial distribution, features and environmental significance of the world’s oceans. They learn about the relationship between ocean currents and climate as well as the variety of marine ecosystems that exist around the world. Students examine the economic, cultural and political dimensions of human interaction with oceans, including issues of ownership, resource use and environmental degradation. They investigate the challenges of managing ocean spaces, including consideration of international treaties, sustainability efforts, and the rights and Knowledge Systems of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and other international Indigenous Peoples.

Key terms

  • biodiversity
  • international waters
  • maritime boundaries
  • navigational rights

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Scale: How oceanic processes operate at different scales, from local marine ecosystems and coastal management to global ocean currents and climate regulation.
  • Sustainability: The need for sustainable ocean management and the role of international cooperation, marine protected areas and Indigenous Practices in protecting marine ecosystems.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How do the physical features and processes of the world’s oceans influence global climate and ecosystems?
  • How do human activities affect the health, value and sustainability of the world’s oceans?
  • What roles do governments, organisations and communities play in managing and protecting ocean environments?
  • How do Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and other Indigenous Communities understand, use and care for ocean environments?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Oceanography content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the physical geography focus areas should enable students to meaningfully investigate natural processes and features in accessible local environments. Where direct observation is not possible, students should investigate how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. In the case of large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, students may access digital technologies to undertake fieldwork and to provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials that explore the diverse physical characteristics of the world’s oceans, marine ecosystems and ocean currents, and human uses and impacts, such as fishing, tourism and conservation.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as allowing access to assistive technology for case study investigations.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate or use their home language(s) or dialect(s) to create word banks for geographical terms.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Oceanography. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Planet Earth

  • Global citizenship

The environmental significance of the world’s oceans links to Global citizenship through sustainable development goals, marine protection and collective responses to overfishing, pollution and climate change.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the natural systems that shape the Earth. They learn about geomorphic and geophysical processes and the roles of water, wind and ice in weathering, erosion and deposition. Students examine climate patterns and factors influencing climate variability. They also learn about biodiversity, ecosystem relationships and human interactions with the environment, including the interactions of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander Peoples or other international Indigenous Peoples.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

Content focus

The School-developed option enables teachers to guide students in developing their knowledge, understanding and skills related to a particular area of interest based on relevant syllabus outcomes. Teachers can plan a school-developed option that considers the needs, strengths, goals, interests and prior learning of their students. This provides opportunities for students to engage with environments, people and places of personal interest and relevance.

Planning a school-developed option

The selected school-developed option should cover a particular area of interest that has not been studied through other core focus areas or options. Students may work as a whole class, in a small group or as individuals.

The content selected for the school-developed option must not overlap or duplicate content from any other NESA syllabus.

The school-developed option should include opportunities for students to:

Suggested areas of interest and focus of study

Geographical concepts

  • Providing students examples of the significance of Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander Peoples and other international Indigenous Peoples in understanding geographical phenomena.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the physical, cultural and economic geography of the Asia-Pacific region. They learn about the diversity of physical environments and how geomorphic and atmospheric processes influence human settlement, access to resources and environmental challenges. Students examine the cultural and historical factors that shape societies across the region, and how demographic, urban and settlement patterns vary between countries. They investigate spatial variations in development, patterns of production and trade, and the economic interdependence between countries in the Asia-Pacific region. Students also consider the role of regional organisations in addressing shared challenges.

Key terms

  • atmospheric processes
  • contemporary geographical issue
  • economic interdependence
  • environmental challenges
  • geomorphic

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Place: The diverse physical and cultural characteristics of countries in the Asia-Pacific region, including variations in landforms, climate, population and cultural identity, and how these influence patterns of human settlement and development.
  • Interconnection: The economic, social and political connections between Australia and its regional neighbours, including trade relationships, migration, development cooperation and shared responses to environmental and social challenges.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How do physical environments and natural processes shape the diversity of landscapes and settlement patterns in the Asia-Pacific region?
  • How do cultural and historical influences shape the identities and settlement patterns of countries in the Asia-Pacific region?
  • What economic patterns and trade connections exist across the Asia-Pacific region, and how do they contribute to regional interdependence?
  • What are the key geographical issues affecting countries in the Asia-Pacific region, and how are different groups responding to these challenges?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Australia’s neighbours content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Large-scale maps and small-scale maps, relief maps, political maps, land use maps, isoline maps, cartogram maps, dot maps, flowline maps, weather maps or synoptic chartsPopulation profiles, scatter plots, bubble charts, line graphs, column graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, remote sensing dataMultimedia, mind maps, cartoons, transects

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as accessing pre-prepared checklists or identification tables to catalogue the diversity of physical environments in the Asia-Pacific region.
  • Encouraging empathy and intercultural understanding by promoting respectful engagement with diverse perspectives and valuing the lived experiences of people in neighbouring countries.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Australia’s neighbours. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Interactions and patterns across a continent

The focus area Australia’s neighbours builds on the study of spatial and cultural diversity examined in Interactions and patterns across a continent and reinforces understanding of environmental influences on settlement and development.

  • Geopolitics

The content of Australia’s neighbours supports and is supported by Geopolitics through shared themes of regional cooperation, political relationships, development and migration patterns.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the geopolitical characteristics of the world, including political systems, sovereignty and the spatial patterns of political affiliation. They learn how political, economic and military powers influence international relations, governance and cooperation. Students examine causes and consequences of political tension and conflict as well as the roles of individuals, groups and governments in promoting peace, resolving disputes and supporting recovery. They investigate how political systems and international organisations contribute to positive change through diplomacy, development and the promotion of human rights.

Key terms

  • diplomacy
  • international cooperation
  • nation-states
  • peacebuilding
  • political affiliations
  • sovereignty

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Space: The spatial organisation and distribution of political systems, power, boundaries and affiliations at local, national and global scales, and how these influence governance, conflict and diplomacy.
  • Environment: The role of global and regional political systems in addressing environmental challenges, managing natural resources and supporting sustainability through cooperation, treaties and international agreements.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How do political systems, nation-states and sovereignty shape global political boundaries and international relations?
  • What factors cause political tension and conflict, and how can they be managed or resolved at different scales?
  • How do international organisations and diplomatic efforts contribute to peacebuilding, development and cooperation?
  • How are global challenges such as environmental sustainability and human rights being addressed through political cooperation and agreements?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Geopolitics content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, political maps, choropleth maps, cartogram maps, dot maps, flowline maps, graduated or proportional symbol mapsClimate graphs, population profiles, bubble chartsVirtual or digital maps, augmented reality, virtual reality, remote sensing dataInfographics, mind maps, cartoons, flow charts, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ Knowledge Systems, digital tools

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials that explore political systems, territorial disputes, conflict and cooperation between nations and spatial patterns of political attitudes or voting behaviours.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as building background knowledge before engaging with case study materials.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.
  • Drawing students’ attention to the representations of some places on maps, such as borders and place names, and how they may be contested by particular communities.
  • Encouraging critical thinking when examining diverse perspectives.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Geopolitics. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Extreme environments

The presence of extreme environments can intensify geopolitical tensions due to competition over resources, territorial claims or challenges related to migration and humanitarian access.

  • Australia’s neighbours

The focus area Australia’s neighbours helps contextualise geopolitical relationships in the Asia-Pacific region, including the influence of political systems, regional cooperation and strategic alliances.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the values and attitudes that underpin global citizenship. They learn about the interdependence of the global economy, the environment and society, and how global challenges such as climate change, inequality and conflict require collective action and international cooperation. Students examine how technology and global connectivity shape global citizenship and how ethical responsibilities influence decisions and actions across a range of scales. Through case studies of global citizenship in action, students investigate initiatives that promote human rights, sustainability and equity, including the contributions of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and other international Indigenous Peoples.

Key terms

  • advocacy
  • environmental stewardship
  • global citizenship
  • global connectivity
  • globalisation
  • intergovernmental organisations

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Interconnection: The interdependence of countries, societies and environments through global trade, environmental issues, migration and shared challenges.
  • Sustainability: The role of global citizens in contributing to sustainable futures by addressing climate change, inequality and responsible resource use.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • What values and attitudes define global citizenship?
  • How do global, economic, environmental and social interdependencies create challenges that require collaborative solutions?
  • In what ways do technologies influence global connectivity and the concept of global citizenship?
  • How can individuals and communities engage in global citizenship to address environmental, social and economic issues?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Global citizenship content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, political maps, choropleth maps, flowline maps, graduated or proportional symbol mapsBubble charts, line graphs, column graphs, bar graphsVirtual or digital maps, global positioning systems (GPS), virtual realityIllustrations, infographics, cartoons, flow charts

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials that explore global interconnections, cultural diversity, international cooperation and shared responsibilities in addressing global challenges such as climate change, inequality or migration.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as by using scaffolds or graphic organisers to connect information from case study materials relating to a global challenge.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.
  • Acknowledging the shared experiences of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples and international Indigenous Peoples such as colonisation, resistance and cultural revitalisation as a foundation to promote global citizenship.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Global citizenship. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Oceanography

Issues of ocean sustainability, climate change and resource exploitation studied in the focus area Oceanography provide real-world contexts for examining ethical dimensions and collective responsibilities of global citizens.

  • Primary production

Global citizenship connects with Primary production through a focus on food security, equitable resource access and sustainable practices in response to global challenges.

Content focus

Students develop an understanding of the role of primary production in providing essential resources, sustaining economies and supporting livelihoods. They learn about the spatial distribution and processes involved in agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry, and learn about global patterns of production. Students investigate the economic significance of primary production, including technological innovations, the influence of multinational organisations and the contribution of primary industries to local and global communities. They consider environmental impacts, challenges related to resource use and sustainable practices that aim to reduce harm and secure future production.

Key terms

  • agriculture
  • fishing
  • forestry
  • mining
  • primary production

Thinking and working geographically

Thinking and working geographically outlines how geographical concepts, inquiry skills and tools can be integrated into each focus area.

Geographical concepts

Suggested opportunities for students to apply geographical concepts are listed below.

  • Space: The distribution of agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry activities and how physical and human factors influence where and how they occur.
  • Sustainability: The environmental, social and economic implications of primary production practices and the need to adopt sustainable approaches to ensure long-term resource security.

Key inquiry questions

Suggested key inquiry questions to support geographical inquiry skills:

  • How does primary production support communities and economies at local, national and global scales?
  • What factors influence the spatial patterns and processes of agriculture, mining, fishing and forestry around the world?
  • What are the environmental, social and economic impacts of primary production and how are they being addressed?
  • How is innovation shaping the future of primary production and what strategies can ensure sustainability in primary production?

Geographical tools

Teachers can select geographical tools that align with Primary production content and their school context. Students with disability may need adjustments when using geographical tools.

MapsData and graphsSpatial technologiesAdditional geographical representations
Special-purpose maps, sketch maps, précis maps, topographic maps, land use maps, cartogram maps, graduated or proportional symbol mapsSector graphs, climate graphsVirtual or digital maps, satellite images, geographic information systems (GIS)Tactile graphics and models, diagrams, flow charts, infographics, sketches

Fieldwork

Fieldwork in the human geography focus areas should allow students to explore how people interact with places, spaces and environments in their local context. Where direct investigation is not possible, such as for large-scale, international or inaccessible locations, accessing digital technologies to undertake fieldwork can provide safe and inclusive opportunities for learning.

Considerations for teaching and learning

  • Providing students with case study materials that explore different types of primary production such as agriculture, forestry, fishing and mining across diverse environments, and highlight environmental impacts, economic significance and sustainability challenges.
  • Providing adjustments for students with disability, such as allowing access to graphic organisers to summarise the impacts of primary industries.
  • Encouraging EAL/D learners to access linguistic supports where appropriate and use their home language(s) or dialect(s) when planning for writing.

Making connections

The focus areas below build on relevant knowledge and skills in Primary production. Below are 2 suggestions for how connections can be made and promote interdisciplinary understanding of physical and human geography.

  • Planet Earth

The focus area Primary production draws on Planet Earth for foundational knowledge of geomorphic processes, climate patterns and ecosystems that influence agricultural, forestry, fishing and mining activities.

  • Global citizenship

The content in Global citizenship provides a lens through which to evaluate the sustainability, equity and global consequences of primary production systems, including ethical food sourcing and environmental stewardship.

seo__description.value: A NSW Education Standards Authority best practice guide for schools to implement Stage 6 assessment practices. Information in this section reflects the NSW standards-referenced framework.

web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Content
web_content_rtb__content.value:
Assessment is used to analyse and interpret the knowledge, understanding and skills that students demonstrate throughout the learning process. Assessment provides information about student learning and achievement at a point in time and the progress students have made.

Assessment is most effective when it is an integral part of teaching and learning. The primary role of assessment is to identify where students are in their learning so that teaching can be adapted to target student needs, and progress can be monitored over time.

Schools use syllabuses, assessment and reporting materials and Assessment Certification and Examination (ACE) requirements to develop school-based assessment programs.

Assessment involves:

  •  identifying where students are in their learning
  •  ongoing monitoring of student progress in relation to the syllabus
  •  providing feedback about student progress to determine the next steps in learning.

Effective school-based assessment:

  • enables students to demonstrate what they know, understand and can do
  • is inclusive of, and accessible for, all students
  • is valid: there is clear alignment between the syllabus, the assessment activity and the criteria used to assess
  • identifies strengths, misunderstandings and skills not yet mastered
  • enables timely and relevant feedback about learning progress
  • provides opportunities for students to reflect on feedback
  • is regular, purposeful and integrated throughout teaching and learning
  • informs goal setting for learning and teaching.

Teachers should evaluate the effectiveness of their assessment approaches regularly to ensure they are fit for purpose. Reviewing student work in relation to assessment activities can provide useful information for decision-making.

Decisions teachers make about teaching, learning and assessment include:

  • what outcomes will be assessed in relation to the content that has been taught
  • why assessment will occur at a point in time and for what purpose
  • how information about student learning will be gathered and what approach will be used
  • how the information will be used, including to provide feedback, and to determine student progress and achievement
  • what next steps will inform future teaching and learning.

Standards-referenced assessment

Standards-referenced assessment refers to the process of interpreting information about student learning in relation to standards. It is used to compare student performance to a standard with objective criteria rather than to the performance of other students. Standards-referenced assessment can provide meaningful feedback about student achievement and support consistent assessment and reporting.

What are standards?

A standards-referenced approach is used to assess and report student achievement in NSW. This approach comprises 2 components:

  • syllabus outcomes and content describe what students are expected to learn
  • how well students demonstrate achievement is described in performance standards such as the Common Grade Scale.

Syllabus outcomes are used by teachers to:

  • plan and develop learning and assessment opportunities in relation to content
  • assess student progress and achievement in relation to intended learning
  • report student progress and achievement at key points in time.

Performance standards used to report student achievement in NSW include:

  • Common Grade Scale (Years 1 to 10)
  • Stage 5 Course Performance Descriptors (end of Year 10)
  • Common Grade Scale for preliminary courses (Year 11)
  • HSC Performance Band Descriptions (Year 12)
  • achievement level descriptions (Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1, and Numeracy).

It is not a requirement for student reports in Early Stage 1 to refer to a performance standard such as a grade scale. More information on standards-referenced reporting is available in Reporting and using grades.

Inclusive assessment

Approaches to assessment should be inclusive of all students. Assessment design should consider the ways students engage in the activity, how information is presented and accessed, and the different ways that students can demonstrate their understanding. Inclusive assessment means ensuring all students are able to demonstrate their learning.

Inclusive assessment considers the following:

  • How students engage:
    • developing accessible learning goals and criteria
    • integrating student choice, for example allowing students to choose topics or contexts in which they demonstrate learning
    • simulating real-life contexts that have explicit relevance to students.
  • How information is presented and accessed, including:
    • resources and/or stimulus material that is presented across a range of modes and that include accessibility options
    • both digital and non-digital resources.
  • How students respond:
    • using self-paced activities that support students to demonstrate learning without time constraints
    • providing opportunities for students to make choices about how they communicate their learning
    • providing opportunities to challenge and/or extend students within their level of understanding.

Adjustments for students with disability

It is a requirement under the Disability Standards for Education 2005 for schools to ensure that assessment tasks are accessible to students with disability. Some students with disability may require adjustments in order to access assessment activities and tasks and to demonstrate their learning. In some cases, this may mean providing an alternative assessment activity. Schools are responsible for any decisions made at school level to offer adjustments to assessment activities and tasks, including in-school tests. Decisions regarding adjustments should be made in the context of collaborative curriculum planning.

  • Summative assessment
  • Evidence and feedback
  • Reporting and using grades
  • Assessment in Stage 6

Checking grades involves reviewing the history of grades allocated by a school to analyse patterns and clarify grading decisions.

When making comparisons, teachers should ensure their grading decisions are based on all available assessment information referenced by relevant grade scales or performance descriptors and published standards.

Schools can use the Grade History Function in Schools Online or the Results Analysis Package to view the grades they have allocated in each course.

Schools can monitor their grade patterns by comparing them to other available data about the performance of students at their school. This will enable schools to have confidence that the grades they intend to allocate are consistent with what they expected from a particular cohort or group of students completing a course.

Principals are accountable for the pattern of grades allocated by their school at the end of Stage 5 and Year 11 courses (except Life Skills and VET) and Year 12 English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and Numeracy CEC. Principals (or their delegates) need to confirm that grades are consistent with published standards when they are submitted.

Related information

  • Assessment in Stage 6

web_content_rtb__content.name: 📜 Content
web_content_rtb__content.value:
Determining grades

A standards-referenced approach is used to report student achievement in NSW. Achievement standards are based on what students are expected to learn and how well they have achieved.

The NSW syllabuses state the intended learning for students by the end of each stage. A to E grade scales describe how well students have achieved. Teachers make professional on-balance judgements to decide which grade description best matches the standards their students have achieved at a particular point in time. These decisions are based on evidence of achievement and information teachers have collected during the teaching and learning.

The A to E grade allocated to a student and reported on NESA credentials reflects the level of achievement demonstrated by the student at the end of the course.

Moderating grades

Teachers follow a process of ‘moderation’ to ensure that grades allocated are consistent with published standards. This means that the grade a student receives in one school can be compared to the same grade anywhere in NSW.

Teachers moderate their judgements by comparing work samples for their students with samples aligned to grades A to E.

Choosing the right grade

Reporting with grades requires that teachers use on-balance judgement in relation to standards. This is a key professional skill.

An on-balance judgement does not just focus on a single piece of work or solely on test results.

Teachers should weigh up the evidence of achievement and other information collected for a student up to that point in time. This information is derived from learning activities, observations and other methods of assessment that are collected over time and in different situations. For further information read our Assessment principles page.

Making on-balance professional judgments involves considering all available evidence of student achievement, with an emphasis on identifying the descriptors that best reflect each student’s performance by the end of the course. Relying solely on marks and predetermined cut scores to allocate grades can lead to inaccuracies, especially for students who demonstrate significant progress over time and are performing at a higher level at the course’s conclusion than they were earlier in the course.

Students with disability

Students with disability may require adjustments to assessment activities to enable access to the activities and equitable opportunity to demonstrate what they know and can do. Students with disability who receive adjustments to assessment activities should have access to the full range of grades.

Using student work samples

Schools can use student work samples to strengthen their understanding of standards. NESA provides limited work samples aligned to A to E grades for a selection of learning areas to assist teachers in understanding state-wide standards. Available work samples can be found with the syllabuses.

Schools can use these published work samples to moderate the grades they allocate to students by comparing the standards of work published with those produced by their students in the same or similar learning areas.

Schools can also use samples of work from their own students for professional development with their staff and/or teachers from other schools. These work samples can provide the basis for professional discussions about standards and ensure there are consistent expectations about student achievement in relation to syllabus outcomes.

Reviewing and improving assessment activities

Referring to student work from previous years may assist teachers to clarify what is expected prior to the grading or marking of student work. Reviewing student work samples may also provide useful information about assessment activities that could lead to improvements in task design. For example, if an assessment activity is found to provide limited opportunities for students to demonstrate achievement at grade A, this could inform future assessment activities so that they are designed with increased scope for students to demonstrate higher levels of knowledge, understanding and skills in relation to the relevant grade scale or achievement level descriptions.

Determining Stage 5 grades

Assessing student achievement is the process of collecting information on student performance in relation to the objectives and outcomes of a course.

In setting activities or tasks, teachers should give careful consideration to the syllabus objectives and outcomes being assessed. By measuring student achievement in relation to these objectives and outcomes, teachers can build up a profile of the achievement of each student in relation to the course performance descriptors.

Grading student achievement is the process of assigning a letter (A, B, C, D, E) to summarise the level of a student's achievement in a course. For students undertaking courses without subject-specific course performance descriptors, that is, Board Endorsed or Content Endorsed Courses, a grade from A to E should be assigned using the Common Grade Scale.

Establishing an assessment program

In establishing an assessment program, teachers should ensure that the types of assessment activities or tasks used are appropriate to the objectives and outcomes being assessed. Generally, it will be necessary to use a number of different assessment activities or tasks in order to ensure that student achievement in relation to all the knowledge and skills objectives is assessed. Principals have the authority to decide on and to implement disability provisions for school-based assessments and tests.

The assessment program should also reflect the relative emphasis placed on the assessable objectives of school programs and the syllabus. For example, where a school has placed considerable emphasis on the development of research skills, that emphasis should be reflected in the assessment program. Objectives from the affective domain (i.e. values and attitudes) should not be used in determining a student's grade.

Where activities or tasks are scheduled throughout a course, greater weight would generally be given to those activities or tasks undertaken towards the end of the course. For example, in a 200-hour course extending over Years 9 and 10, the assessment information collected in Year 10 provides the more complete picture of student achievement. There are, however, a number of different ways of organising the teaching/learning program for a course. The scheduling of activities or tasks and the weights applied should reflect the course organisation. Students should be given the opportunity to demonstrate their maximum level of achievement relative to the course performance descriptors.

Applying the course performance descriptors

Course performance descriptors have been developed for each course. They describe the main features of a typical student's performance at each grade measured against the syllabus objectives and outcomes for the course.

Teachers will make the final judgement of the most appropriate grade on the basis of all available assessment information and with reference to the course performance descriptors. In applying these descriptors, teachers should interpret them in terms of standards that can be achieved by Stage 5 students within the bounds of the course. The same course performance descriptors apply to 100-hour and 200-hour courses. This relates to courses studied across Years 9 and 10, and to courses studied exclusively in either Year 9 or Year 10.

The grades allocated should reflect the relative emphasis placed on the assessable objectives of school programs and the syllabus. For example, where a school has placed considerable emphasis on the development of research skills, that emphasis should be reflected in the assessment program. Objectives from the affective domain (i.e. values and attitudes) should not be used in determining a student's grade.

Advice for Year 12: English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and Numeracy CEC

Schools must allocate to students who complete Year 12 English Studies or Mathematics Standard 1, or Numeracy CEC the grade that reflects their achievement at the end of the course. This grade is reported on the student’s HSC Record of Achievement.

To ensure grades have consistent meaning across the state, NESA monitors the grades allocated and reviews student work samples provided by schools.

Checklist for schools

This checklist relates to Year 12 grades that are reported on students' NESA credentials.

1. Read the Achievement Level Descriptions

Familiarise yourself with the Achievement Level Descriptions, on the syllabus page for the relevant course.

  • English Studies Achievement Level Descriptions
  • Mathematics Standard 1 Achievement Level Descriptions
  • Numeracy CEC Achievement Level Descriptions

2. Review work samples

Samples of student work aligned to grades are provided on the syllabus page. Use the samples and their annotations to get a clear understanding of the standard at each grade.

3. Upload grades and work samples

  • Decide on the appropriate grade for each student based on the achievement they have demonstrated at the end of the course.
  • Enter student grades in Schools Online.
  • Upload student work samples and the associated assessment activities in Schools Online.

Schools Online has guides on how to enter grades and upload student work samples. Learn more about submitting work samples.

4. Confirm grades

Check the grades entered in Schools Online are correct before they are confirmed by the principal.

5. Revise grades

Schools may be contacted by NESA and asked to revise grades. If your school is contacted, you will have a short period of time to make changes.

6. Keep grades confidential

NESA monitors grades before they are finalised and released to students. School assessment grades are available to students in Students Online once the final HSC exam has ended. Do not reveal grades to students before this time.

Related information

  • Assessment in Stage 6

Formal school-based assessment in Stage 6

Schools will use school-based assessment requirements, included in course specific assessment and reporting materials, to develop a formal assessment program for each course. Formal assessment programs must also comply with requirements outlined in Assessment Certification Examination and the schools’ assessment policies and procedures for Stage 6.

Schools are required to provide written advice to students about the schools’ requirements for assessment including:

  • formal assessment schedules at the commencement of each Year 11 and Year 12 course
  • each formal assessment task.

The assessment policies must include statements of school procedures relating to:

  • organisational details of the school’s assessment program for each course, giving the:
    • number and types of assessment tasks
    • components and weightings
    • scheduling of the tasks.
  • marking, recording and reporting student achievement in assessment tasks
  • administrative arrangements associated with:
    • absence from an assessment task
    • late submission of tasks due to illness or misadventure, malpractice and invalid or unreliable tasks.
  • student appeals against assessment rankings
  • ‘N’ determinations.

Formal assessment schedule 

Prior to the commencement of a course, teachers must develop an assessment schedule identifying formal assessment opportunities for students to demonstrate their achievement at certain points in the course.

The purpose of a formal assessment schedule is to provide an overview of course components and component weightings, and the number, type, timing and weighting of each task.

When developing a formal assessment schedule, teachers:

  • use course-specific assessment and reporting materials to ensure the mandatory course components and component weightings are addressed
  • provide opportunities for a range of task types that allow students to demonstrate what they know and can do in relation to course outcomes
  • identify the appropriate timing of tasks in relation to the teaching and learning cycle, being mindful of the demands these tasks will place on students and teachers
  • plan for assessment of a range of course outcomes, recognising that there is no requirement to formally assess all course content areas, topics or modules.

Measures of outcomes that address values and attitudes, or measures that reflect student conduct, should not be included in formal school-based assessment. Schools may choose to report on these separately.

There is no requirement for assessment schedules to include tasks with a greater weighting towards the end of the course.

Course components and component and weightings 

Components for assessment include the course knowledge, understanding and skills. The weightings of components are consistent with their emphasis in the course.

Teachers plan each assessment task to reflect one or more related components. This ensures that assessment in relation to outcomes occurs across the course in a manageable way using a range of task types.

The components and weightings indicated in a formal assessment schedule will provide a framework for an assessment task type. The task types used must be appropriate to the components of the course being assessed.

The weighting of a component does not need to reflect the mark allocation assigned to a task. For example, an assessment task may be weighted in an assessment schedule at 20%. To provide a mark range that allows for discrimination between the performances of individual students, the maximum marks to be awarded for the task may be 30. This will be reflected in the marking guidelines. To maintain the task’s stated weighting, schools may consider using statistical methods when aggregating marks.

A range of sample formal assessment schedules are available for Stage 6 courses. Schools may choose to use a sample without amendment or make changes.

Formal assessment notification

Schools are required to provide students with written advice about the formal assessment requirements for each course.

For each formal task, schools must provide:

  • adequate written notification in advance of the task (typically, 2 weeks)
  • details of the task, including:
    • task number
    • timing
    • outcomes assessed
    • description of the nature of the task
    • marking criteria
    • feedback to be provided.

The task number, timing and outcomes must reflect the assessment schedule for a course.

The nature of the task should clearly describe for students the requirements and expectations of the task.

Marking criteria for the task should outline for students what will be assessed in relation to the outcomes.

Feedback will be provided to students relating to their performance in the task that provides meaningful and useful information relative to the achievement of outcomes. Where appropriate, marking guidelines should be provided at the time of the written notification.

Malpractice

Malpractice is:

  • any dishonest behaviour and/or attempt to gain an unfair advantage over other students, and/or  
  • knowingly assisting other students to engage in malpractice.

For detailed information on malpractice and how it is treated read Malpractice in HSC exams and HSC minimum standard tests.

School reports 

Teachers are to refer to information and advice provided by their school or sector about specific requirements for reporting to parents and carers. For more information go to Reporting and Using Grades. 

End of course reporting to NESA

Year 11

Schools are responsible for allocating a grade to each student who completes a Year 11 course (except Life Skills and VET courses) to represent their achievement at the end of the course. These grades are determined by the student’s performance in relation to the Common Grade Scale for Preliminary courses. Teachers make professional, on-balance judgements about which grade description best matches the standards their students have demonstrated by the end of the course. Using a computer program, an algorithm or numeric data to determine grades is not considered best practice.

Teachers are required to ensure that the grades allocated are consistent with published standards. This means that the grade a student receives in one school can be compared to the same grade anywhere in NSW. To ensure judgements are consistent with statewide standards, teachers compare their students’ work with relevant work samples on the NESA website that are aligned to the A to E Common Grade Scale for Preliminary courses. The grade allocated is reported on a student’s Record of School Achievement (RoSA), a credential that allows students to accumulate their academic results until they leave school. It is also reported on their HSC credential.

Providing adjustments to assessment tasks for a student with disability does not restrict the student’s access to the full range of grades.

Year 12

Schools are responsible for providing information to NESA about student performance in school-based assessments. The type of information that is provided to NESA depends on the course. The Assessment and Reporting documents located on the syllabus page for each course detail the requirements.

Grades

Schools use Achievement Level Descriptions to allocate grades (A to E) to all students who complete Year 12 courses in English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and Numeracy CEC. The grades allocated to students for school-based assessment in these courses will be reported on HSC credentials.

Students who leave school prior to the Higher School Certificate examinations will receive a RoSA. It records grades for their completed Stage 5 and Year 11 courses and any participation in Stage 6 courses that were not completed.

Providing adjustments to assessment tasks for a student with disability does not restrict the student’s access to the full range of grades.

Final assessment marks

Schools submit a final assessment mark for each Board Developed course a student completes (other than Life Skills, VET and English Studies and Mathematics Standard 1 courses). At the conclusion of the assessment program, schools add up each student’s assessment marks for each task, ensuring that the components and weightings in the assessment information for the course have been applied. To enable moderated school assessment marks to provide an accurate representation of student performance, it is important that marks submitted to NESA establish the rank order and reflect the relative differences between students' achievement in the course.

Providing adjustments to assessment tasks for a student with disability does not restrict the student’s access to the full range of marks.

Schools can advise students of their rank order in each course, but must not inform students of their final, cumulative, school-based assessment mark as these marks will be moderated based on examination performance and aligned to the performance standards. Students can access their Assessment Rank Order Notice in Students Online after the last HSC examination. If a student thinks that the rank order is not correct, they can seek advice from the school about the rank order appeal process.

Estimated marks

NESA requires schools to submit an estimated examination mark for all students entered for optional HSC examinations in English Studies, Mathematics Standard 1 and VET framework courses. This mark is an estimate of likely performance in the HSC examination and reflects the student’s achievement on a task or tasks similar to the HSC examination, such as a trial HSC examination. The estimated examination mark should not be revealed to students as it is only used in the case of a successful illness/misadventure application.

VET courses

Schools will provide information about student performance in relation to VET course requirements.

VET courses are delivered by a registered training organisation (RTO). The RTO determines the unit of competency outcomes for students.

Schools must work with the delivering RTO to submit the competency outcomes via Schools Online (unless the student is studying the course through TAFE NSW). Where applicable, work placement hours are also recorded.

Students receive recognition towards their school qualification (RoSA or HSC), as well as a nationally recognised VET qualification (Certificate or Statement of Attainment). NESA distributes these qualifications on behalf of the school sector RTOs. TAFE NSW and other providers issue their own qualifications.

Life Skills outcomes

Where students satisfactorily complete a Life Skills course in Years 10–12, schools report to NESA the outcomes achieved by the student, either independently or with support. These outcomes are recorded on the Profile of Student Achievement and issued along with other credentials when the student leaves school.

The school will keep a record of the outcomes achieved by the student.
